speaker_role: independent counselor/financial aid consultant (self-described former law school and college admissions application reader turned financial aid consultant, 'Coach David' of Eagle Financial Aid, formerly branded Financial Aid Secrets)
commercial_incentive: Yes - heavily promotes his paid consulting services throughout (phone/text numbers repeated, QR code for booking, pricing urgency, testimonials of dollar savings)
key_insights: The CSS Profile goes far beyond the FAFSA, also asking about home equity/market value, retirement account balances, non-retirement annuities, medical spending accounts, sibling assets, and other valuables the FAFSA ignores

Presenter argues families should only answer required CSS Profile questions and skip every optional question, since he claims volunteering extra financial detail tends to reduce aid rather than increase it

He recommends using the county tax assessor's valuation for home market value rather than current market/Zillow-style value, arguing colleges otherwise inflate perceived home equity using unrealized appreciation

For separated/divorced families, non-custodial parent financial information can still be requested by CSS Profile schools even when that parent isn't part of the student's life, which is the subject of an active lawsuit against a group of colleges
First-year baseline asset/income snapshot is described as most consequential, so major asset changes (e.g., buying a home) are advised to be timed to avoid the first CSS Profile filing year
Presenter claims certain asset types (e.g., physical gold) are not directly asked about on the CSS Profile, implying a reporting gap families could exploit
CSS Profile filing opens in fall of the student's senior year (technically around October 1) and is run by the College Board, used by roughly 400+ colleges
A family earning under $100,000 may be eligible for a CSS Profile fee waiver per this presenter's description of the form
specific_numbers_or_facts: Presenter states about 18 colleges settled a lawsuit over CSS Profile financial-aid practices for roughly $250 million combined; a second related lawsuit is described as ongoing
Presenter claims the CSS Profile has roughly 5x as many questions as the FAFSA, across 17 sections

Presenter cites unverified consulting-outcome examples: saved a $350k-income family $35,000-$37,000 at private schools, saved a $400k-income family $40,000 at Baylor, saved a $230k-income family over $30,000
Presenter states a student must be age 24+ to be considered an independent student for financial aid purposes
Presenter says the CSS Profile financial-aid 'look-back' period uses tax returns from two years prior
notable_or_distinctive: The line-by-line CSS Profile walkthrough with specific tactical advice (skip optional questions, use assessed rather than market home value, avoid gold/cash-equivalent reporting gaps, time home purchases around the base year) is more granular and actionable than typical financial aid content.
reliability_notes: This is a sales webinar for a paid financial-aid consulting service; the tactical advice to withhold or minimize volunteered information and interpretive claims about a lawsuit ('why would they settle unless they were guilty') reflect the presenter's opinion/sales framing rather than verified fact, and dollar-savings testimonials are unverifiable self-reported claims.
